rationale: Both passages date Cyrus's written proclamation to his first year and expressly connect the stirring of his spirit with fulfillment of the Lord's word through Jeremiah.
Ezra explicitly invokes Jeremiah's fulfilled word; the prophet promises a return from Babylon when seventy years are fulfilled. The actual Greek reference is Jeremiah 36:10.
Cyrus's declaration that the God of heaven gave him the kingdoms and commanded a house in Jerusalem is also recorded in Chronicles' closing proclamation.
Both proclamations invite God's people to go up with God accompanying them; Ezra expressly continues with the rebuilding of the Jerusalem house.
The command to rebuild Jerusalem's temple under Cyrus corresponds to Isaiah's explicit naming of Cyrus alongside the promise that Jerusalem and the holy house will be rebuilt.
The instruction that neighbours support the returnees with precious metals, belongings and livestock is followed by those neighbours supplying those named categories and freewill gifts.

The returnees arise because God stirs their spirits to build, resembling Haggai's later description of the spirits of Zerubbabel, Joshua and the people being stirred to resume work; the stages of the project differ.

relationship: Royal support instruction carried out; same-chapter
rationale: The neighbours' provision of silver, gold, belongings and livestock carries out the concrete support requested in Cyrus's proclamation.
The restoration of vessels removed by Nebuchadnezzar reverses the Babylonian removal of the sanctuary's utensils, including gold and silver bowls; the individual inventories are not made identical.
The recovered royal memorandum expressly orders the return to Jerusalem of gold and silver vessels carried to Babylon, the reversal narrated under Cyrus here.
Both passages name Sasabasar as the recipient of vessels restored by Cyrus; the titles differ, ruler of Judah here and treasury keeper there, and neither is silently substituted for Mithradates.

The vessels' journey with Sasabasar from Babylon to Jerusalem is recalled in the elders' report of Cyrus entrusting him with the vessels and directing their return; the target does not repeat the 5400 total.
Ezra's introduction to the returnees from Nebuchadnezzar's deportation corresponds to the register Nehemiah says he found of those who had come up first.

Both registers begin with Zorobabel and list leaders before the numbered households, including Neemias, Mardochaios and Baana. The lists have different additional names and forms, so the entries are not silently equated person by person.
Both return registers list Phoros with 2172; the family name and count agree.
Both registers list Saphatia with 372, preserving the same named household and total.
Both name Era, but Ezra gives 775 and Nehemiah 652; the parallel entry is retained with the numerical difference.
Both list Phaathmoab and the Iesoue/Jesus and Ioab/Joab grouping, but the totals are 2812 here and 2818 there; the source name forms and figures remain distinct.
Both registers list Ailam with 1254, an exact name-and-count correspondence.
Both list Zathoua, with 945 in Ezra and 845 in Nehemiah; neither total is corrected to match the other.
Both registers give Zakchou a total of 760.
Both registers name Banoui, but the recorded totals differ, 642 here and 648 there.

The parallel family-list section has Babi with 623 here and Bebi with 628 there. The differing spelling and count are preserved as record variants, without claiming that spelling alone proves family identity.
Both registers name Asgad, but Ezra records 3222 and Nehemiah 2322; the thousand-person difference is preserved.
The parallel entries read Adonikam with 666 here and Adenikam with 667 there; both the spelling and total differ and are left as written.
Both registers list Bagoi, with 2056 in Ezra and 2067 in Nehemiah.
The parallel section lists Adin with 454 here and Edin with 655 there; the two names and totals are compared as written, not reconciled into one numerical claim.
Both entries identify Ater in relation to Ezekia and give 98, a correspondence in both the identifying phrase and count.
Ezra's Bethlehem entry gives 123, matching the Baithleem entry in Nehemiah's combined Bethlehem-Netopha source unit; the place-name forms are preserved.
Both registers give Netopha 56; Nehemiah includes it in the same actual source unit as Baithleem, rather than a separate verse.
Both registers list Anathoth with 128.
The corresponding locality entries are Asmoth and Bethasmoth, each with 42; the added place-name element is retained rather than silently removed.
Both registers group Kariathiarim, Kaphira and Beroth together and give 743.
Both registers group Arama and Gabaa together and give 621.
The parallel locality entries read Machmas and Machemas, each with 122; the source spellings remain as printed.
Both name Bethel and Aia together, but Ezra gives 423 and Nehemiah 123.
The corresponding locality section gives Nabou and Nabi-aar, each with 52; this is a comparison of the register entries, not proof from the shared number alone that every name element is identical.
Elam-ar here and Elam-aar there each have 1254 in the corresponding part of the locality list; the spelling distinction is retained.
Both registers give Eram 320 in the locality section, distinct from the later priestly entry with a similar name.
Both group Lod and Ono with a third locality, but that middle name is Aroth here and Adid there, and the totals are 725 and 721.
Both registers give Jericho 345; its position relative to the Lod group differs.
Both name Sanaa, with 3630 in Ezra and 3930 in Nehemiah.
Both priestly sections begin with a house associated with Iesous/Jesus and a count of 973, but the head name is Iedoua here and Jodae there; the wording is not normalized.
Both priestly lists give Emmer 1052.
Both priestly lists give Phassour 1247.
The corresponding priestly entries read Erem with 1007 here and Eram with 1017 there; both name form and count differ, and this is not confused with the locality Eram entry.
Both Levitical entries give 74 and include Iesous/Jesus, Kadmiel and Odouia/Oudouia; the different wording of their relationships is preserved rather than made into a single exact genealogy.
Both identify the singers as sons of Asaph, but give 128 in Ezra and 148 in Nehemiah.
Both gatekeeper lists share Saloum, Ater, Telmon, Akoub and Atita; the last name is Sabaou versus Sabi, and the totals are 139 versus 138.
Both begin the Nathinim section with a three-name group ending in Tabaoth; Ezra has Souia and Asouphe, while Nehemiah has Sea and Asipha, preserving their differing forms.
The next groups both end in Phadon, with Keraos and Soea here and Kiras and Souia there; the comparison rests on the parallel register section, not a forced identification of every spelling.
Both sections contain Labano/Labana and Agaba, but Ezra's third name is Akaboth while Nehemiah's is Salami. Those two names are not equated.
Ezra lists Agab, Samalai and Anan in this unit; the parallel Nehemiah section includes Salami and Anan across two units but does not repeat this exact three-name group.
Ezra's Kedel, Gaer and Reea are compared with Gadel, Gaar and Raaia in the parallel sequence, which crosses a verse boundary in Nehemiah; the forms are retained without inventing an exact genealogy.
Both sections contain Rason and Nekoda, followed by Gazem here and Gezam there; Nehemiah divides the group across two actual units.
The parallel sequence reads Ousa, Phase and Basi here, and Ozi, Phese and Besi there, crossing a Nehemiah verse boundary; the spelling differences remain explicit.

The neighbouring register section places Asena, Maonim and Naphison before Bakbouk here, while Nehemiah has Besi, Meinom and Nephosasim before Bakbouk. Asena is not identified as Besi merely by position.
Both groups include Bakbouk and Arour, with Akipha here and Achipha there; the same three-entry pattern is retained with its spelling difference.
Both groups begin with Basaloth, but continue with Maouda and Aresa here versus Meida and Adasan there; the varying names are not silently replaced.
Both registers give the same three names in this group: Barkous, Sisara and Thema.
The closing Nathinim pair is Nasoue and Atoupha here, Nisia and Atipha there; the parallel section is compared without asserting that the differing spellings themselves prove individual identity.

Ezra's next section is labelled sons of Abdeselma and lists Sati, Asepherath and Phadoura; Nehemiah labels its corresponding section sons of Salomon's slaves and lists Souti, Sapharath and Pherida. The labels and names are preserved separately.
The parallel three-name groups are Ieela, Darkon and Gedel here and Jeale, Dorkon and Gadel there; this is a register comparison, not an added biographical identification.
Both groups begin with Saphatia and continue with Atil/Etil and Emi/Emim, but Ezra has the combined form Phacherath-aseboin where Nehemiah separately lists Phacharath and Sabaim.
Both registers give 392 for the combined Nathinim and following servant-family groups, despite the differing Abdeselma and Salomon's-slaves section labels.
Both lists introduce returnees unable to prove Israelite descent, naming Thelmeleth and Charoub among their origins; the other place forms differ and remain as written.
Both list Dalaia, Tobia and Nekoda among those with unverified descent, but Ezra also includes Boua and gives 652, while Nehemiah gives 642.
Both priestly lists describe a Berzellai/Berzelli name acquired through marriage into the Galaadite family; the other names and the singular wife/plural wives wording differ.
Both accounts state that the missing genealogical record led to exclusion from the priesthood on grounds of descent.
Both have Athersatha prohibit eating the holiest food until a priest can provide divine illumination; Ezra adds the perfect things, while Nehemiah says the priest will give light.
Both registers give the whole assembly as 42360; this agreement does not silently reconcile differences in the component entries.
Both give 7337 male and female slaves, but the additional male and female singers number 200 here and 245 in Nehemiah.
Both inventories record 736 horses and 245 mules.
Both inventories record 435 camels and 6720 donkeys.

Both accounts record contributions for the work after the returnee register; Nehemiah divides gifts among contributor groups, while Ezra's notice introduces the leaders' freewill offerings for the house.

Both accounts inventory gold, silver and priestly garments for the work, but their allocations, stated units and totals differ; Ezra's 61000 gold minas, 5000 silver minas and 100 garments are not converted into Nehemiah's figures.
Both registers conclude that priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants and the people settled in their towns; Nehemiah then adds the arrival of the seventh month.

The anticipated illuminating and perfect things concern priestly discernment, resembling the Manifestation and Truth placed on Aaron's judgment-piece; the expressions in the supplied translation have a related function but are not silently made the same wording.
Both accounts place the returned Israelites in their towns when the seventh month arrives; Ezra proceeds to their gathering in Jerusalem, while Nehemiah continues into its own assembly narrative.
Ezra expressly grounds the rebuilt altar's whole burnt offerings in Moses' law; Exodus prescribes continual altar offerings with a lamb morning and evening.
The restored morning and evening whole burnt offerings follow the specific daily schedule commanded for the altar in Exodus.
The returned people keep Booths according to what is written; Leviticus specifies the seventh-month Feast of Tents, its seven days, offerings and eighth-day assembly.
Numbers gives the first and second days' prescribed numbers for the seventh-month festival, illustrating Ezra's statement that each day's offerings followed the required count.

Ezra's regular and new-moon offerings correspond to the law's continual daily sacrifices and its separately prescribed monthly offerings; the target does not exhaust every festival and freewill category named in Ezra.
Food, drink and oil exchanged for Lebanon timber brought to Joppa resemble Solomon's arrangements with Tyre; Cyrus's rebuilding concession and the earlier royal contract are distinct.
Appointing Levites twenty years old and upward to temple work corresponds to the age threshold recorded in David's final arrangements for Levitical service.
Ezra names Asaph's descendants with cymbals and explicitly appeals to David's directions; Chronicles describes David appointing Asaph's family among the musicians for temple praise.
Priests with trumpets and Asaph-associated Levites with cymbals at the foundation resemble the musical combination at Solomon's temple ceremony, without equating foundation and dedication.

Ezra's thanksgiving includes the refrain that His mercy toward Israel endures for ever, closely corresponding to the psalm's opening call to thanksgiving for the Lord's kindness and enduring mercy; Ezra says that it is good, rather than using the psalm's exact wording.

relationship: Former house compared with the present
rationale: Ezra's elders weep when comparing the former house with the new work; Haggai explicitly addresses those who saw its former glory and urges strength despite the present appearance. The scenes occur at different stages.

The would-be builders appeal to Assyrian resettlement and worship of Israel's God; Kings narrates settlement in Samaria and a mixed form of worship. Its Assyrian king is unnamed here, so he is not identified as Asaraddon from this passage alone.
The leaders expressly appeal to Cyrus's command authorizing the return and rebuilding, the commission recorded in the opening proclamation.
Both descriptions say opponents sought to weaken the builders' hands and stop their work; Nehemiah concerns the wall project, not the identical obstruction of the temple narrated here.

The notice that opposition lasted until Darius's reign is resumed in the statement that temple work remained idle until his second year; the intervening letters about the city are not flattened into one continuous royal reign.
Both accounts describe foreign populations settled in Samaria's cities by royal deportation; the target does not name Asennaphar, and the named deportation lists are not assumed to be identical.

The accusation that Jerusalem's builders are reviving a rebellious city resembles the later charge that Nehemiah's wall building conceals rebellion; Nehemiah expressly denies that charge, and the letters are separate.
The warning that a rebuilt city would withhold taxes is answered by the king's reference to earlier tribute and his order to stop rebuilding to prevent harm to rulers.

relationship: Archive search requested and reported; same-chapter
rationale: The accusers request a search of royal records, and the royal reply states that a search was ordered and reports its finding of prior revolt.

The royal reply's reference to earlier revolt has a concrete historical analogue in Sedekias breaking faith with Babylon; Kings is not identified as the Persian archive record, nor does that past event prove current rebellion.

The reply recalls Jerusalem's mighty kings ruling west of the river; the Kings passage describes Solomon ruling the region beyond the River from Raphi to Gaza. It supports the former extent of rule, not every tax claim in the letter.
The king's instruction to stop the city builders is followed by the officials hurrying to Jerusalem and stopping them with force.
The officials' forceful intervention carries out the royal order to halt rebuilding and guard against slackness; it is not the later decision of Darius permitting temple work.
Ezra places the temple's inactivity before the second year of Darius; Haggai dates his rebuke to that same regnal year and commands the people to rebuild the desolate house.

Ezra's notice of Haggai's prophecy over the rebuilding community corresponds to the dated oracle addressed to Zerubbabel and Joshua in Darius's second year; the source and target use different forms of those leaders' names.
Ezra's Zacharias son of Addo corresponds to the prophetic heading naming Zechariah, Berechiah's son, son of Addo, in Darius's second year; the fuller genealogy is preserved rather than omitted.
Haggai describes Zerubbabel, Joshua and the people responding to the prophet and returning to work, the concrete response summarized when Ezra says the leaders began building with the prophets' help.
The rebuilding begun with Haggai and Zacharias helping is later described as advancing through those same prophets' prophecy toward completion.
The question who authorized the building is repeated in the officials' written report to Darius, identifying the same inquiry within the narrative.

relationship: Names requested and purpose explained; same-chapter
rationale: The request for the builders' names is repeated in the letter, which explains that the officials wanted to report the names of their leaders to the king.
The work continues while Darius considers the report, and his eventual order directs the officials to leave the work alone and supply its costs; the later letter resolves the pending inquiry.
The governor Thanthanai and Satharbouzana who send the inquiry are named again when they implement Darius's reply diligently.
The report of stone and timber construction can be compared with the recovered decree specifying strong stone courses and a wooden course; the report does not itself state those course counts.

relationship: Inquiry recalled in the letter; same-chapter
rationale: The officials' letter repeats their earlier question concerning the authority to rebuild the house.
The officials explain in writing the request for names already reported when they visited the builders.
The elders recall a great Israelite king building the former house; Solomon explicitly states that he built the house promised to David's son in Kings.
The elders' account of Babylon destroying the house and deporting the people corresponds to the burning of the temple and removal of Jerusalem's remaining people under Nebuchadnezzar's officer.
The elders explain the disaster as a result of the ancestors provoking God; Chronicles connects priestly and popular unfaithfulness with Babylonian destruction and exile.
The elders' appeal to Cyrus's first-year decision recalls the dated written proclamation and explicit rebuilding commission opening Ezra.

Both accounts describe Cyrus restoring the vessels taken from Jerusalem and giving them to Sasabasar; his title differs between the accounts, and Mithradates remains the official handling the count in the opening narrative.
The instruction reported to Sasabasar corresponds to the recovered decree directing the gold and silver vessels to be returned to their place in Jerusalem's sanctuary.

The elders attribute laying the foundation to Sasabasar, while the earlier narrative describes foundation work led by Zorobabel and Iesous. Both concern the temple rebuilding, but the passages do not establish that Sasabasar and Zorobabel are the same person.

The request for a search concerning Cyrus's decree is followed by Darius ordering a search and the discovery of a memorandum of that decree; the scroll is found in a Median citadel, not simply assumed found in Babylon.
